title: An introduction to cosmology
one_line_summary: Opens Part III by arguing that gravity controls the largest scales, adopting the cosmological principle at scales above about 100 Mpc, turning Hubble's law into a scale factor a(t) with comoving coordinates, building cosmic time from a foliation by spacelike slices threaded by Weyl's fundamental observers, writing the general comoving metric, and then solving two toy universes: empty Minkowski space (Universe 0) and the spatially flat, exponentially expanding de Sitter model driven purely by a cosmological constant (Universe 1).
role_in_book: First chapter of Part III. Part II ended with the field equation (ch13) and its weak-field and Schwarzschild consequences (ch14); this chapter is the first place the full equation, including Lambda, is applied to a whole spacetime rather than to a star. It sets up the kinematic language (homogeneity, isotropy, scale factor, comoving observers, cosmic time) and gives a first taste of the recipe used through Part III: guess a symmetric metric, compute curvature (here via the orthonormal frame and vielbein from ch10-11), and match against an energy-momentum content. The general spatial geometries (k = -1, 0, +1) are deferred to ch16, realistic matter to ch17, a zoo of models to ch18, and horizons and conformal infinity to ch19; the de Sitter horizon and light-cone narrowing are only previewed in exercises and margin notes.

assumed_background.topic: Einstein field equation with cosmological constant, and the vacuum energy-momentum tensor
Perfect fluid and dust energy-momentum tensors
Riemann tensor, its symmetries, Ricci tensor and scalar
Orthonormal frames, vielbeins, raising and lowering with eta in a local frame
Connection coefficients from the metric and the geodesic equation
Line elements, spherical polar coordinates, metric signature (-,+,+,+)
Astronomical unit, light-year, parallax, galaxies and the cosmic microwave background as observational notions
Four fundamental interactions and why like charges cancel in electromagnetism

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why gravity, although the weakest interaction, dominates the dynamics of the Universe on large scales (long range, only attractive, additive).
Reader can state the cosmological principle, separate homogeneity from isotropy, and explain why it fails locally but holds after coarse-graining on scales of roughly 100 Mpc.
Reader can convert between AU, light-years and parsecs and place stars, galaxies and the homogeneity scale on a ladder of distances.
Reader can derive v = H r from uniform scaling r(t) = a(t) r(t0), show it holds for every observer, and identify H(t) = a-dot/a.
Reader can distinguish comoving from physical coordinates and Hubble flow from peculiar (proper) motion, and give the CMB dipole as an example of the latter.
Reader can describe a foliation of spacetime by spacelike hypersurfaces, define cosmic time and comoving observers, and state Weyl's postulate.
Reader can argue from isotropy that fluid world lines must be orthogonal to the slices (g_{0i} = 0) and use the vanishing of Gamma^i_{00} to test that coordinates are comoving.
Reader can write the general comoving homogeneous-isotropic line element ds^2 = -dt^2 + a^2 gamma_ij dx^i dx^j and say what a(t) and gamma_ij encode.
Reader can show that Minkowski spacetime solves the empty-universe Einstein equation and explain why Ricci-flat does not in general mean Riemann-flat.
Reader can compute the orthonormal-frame Riemann and Ricci components, and the Ricci scalar R = 6(a-ddot/a + a-dot^2/a^2), for the spatially flat expanding metric.
Reader can solve the 00 component of the Einstein equation with only Lambda to obtain a(t) = exp(Ht) with H^2 = Lambda/3, and check the spatial components.
Reader can interpret a positive cosmological constant as a fluid with rho = Lambda/8pi and p = -rho, and explain (with the correct GR reason) why it drives accelerated expansion.

teaching_approach.summary: A short, bridging chapter that moves from physical motivation and order-of-magnitude astronomy to kinematic geometry and then to a single computed solution. The authors first make the simplifying assumption plausible by zooming out through distance scales, then derive Hubble's law as a consequence of uniform rescaling so that it no longer seems to put us at the centre. Geometry is introduced pictorially (stacked sheets pierced by world lines) before being turned into metric conditions. The two model universes are deliberately minimal: an empty one that is just Minkowski space in disguise, and one with only vacuum energy, where the curvature computation doubles as practice with the orthonormal frame machinery of ch10. The chapter ends with an intuitive (and somewhat loose) negative-pressure story and defers generality to later chapters.
narrative_arc: Why gravity: compare the four interactions and argue that long range plus no cancellation makes gravity the ruler of cosmic structure; flag cosmic evolution (good news) and singularities (bad news).
Goal: solve Einstein's equation with Lambda for the whole matter content, which means finding a metric everywhere.
Simplify: Copernican principle leads to the cosmological principle (homogeneity plus isotropy).

Reality check: the principle is obviously false in daily life and in the Solar System and Galaxy; a distance ladder (AU, ly, pc, kpc, Mpc) shows lumpiness smoothing out above about 100 Mpc, so matter is coarse-grained into a perfect cosmic fluid.

Observation: Hubble's law; resolve the apparent 'we are the centre' paradox by uniform scaling, introducing a(t), H = a-dot/a, comoving versus physical coordinates, Hubble flow versus proper motions, and the CMB dipole.
Scope limit: bound systems like the Solar System ignore the expansion; Part III looks only at the largest scales.
Geometry: cosmic time via a foliation by spacelike hypersurfaces on which the cosmological principle holds; comoving observers pierce the slices.
Constraints: isotropy forces slices orthogonal to fluid world lines, giving g_{0i}=0, e_0=u, g_00=-1; Gamma^i_{00}=0 identifies comoving coordinates; Weyl's postulate enshrines the geodesic bundle.
General comoving metric with a(t) and gamma_ij (Robertson-Walker form previewed).
Universe 0: T=0, show Minkowski solves it, geodesics are straight lines; caveat that Ricci-flat need not be flat.
Universe 1: spatially flat expanding metric; compute curvature in the orthonormal frame, transform back with the vielbein, get R.
Match with pure vacuum energy: 00 equation gives exponential expansion with H^2 = Lambda/3; interpret Lambda as negative pressure.
Summary and exercises that preview constant curvature, cosmological horizons, redshifting of momenta and the vacuum-energy problem.
signature_moves: Admits the central assumption is 'clearly wrong' and then rescues it by a zoom-out through distance scales, making coarse-graining the explicit justification.
Defuses the anthropocentric reading of Hubble's law by using separation vectors r_i - r_j, so the origin drops out.
Pictures cosmic time as a stack of paper-like sheets pierced by a bundle of arrows before writing any metric component.
Uses isotropy to exclude a tilt between world lines and slices (a tilt would single out a direction), turning a symmetry statement into g_{0i}=0.
Gives a practical diagnostic for comoving coordinates: check that g_{00,i} and g_{0i,0} vanish so Gamma^i_{00} = 0 and particles at rest stay at rest.
Numbers its toy models (Universe 0, Universe 1) to build a ladder of increasingly realistic universes continued in ch18.
Recycles the cosmological example as practice with the orthonormal frame and vielbein, spelling out every sign from eta when raising and lowering.
Reads the cosmological constant back as a perfect fluid with an effective negative pressure to give a physical story for acceleration.
Pushes the full connection and Riemann calculation into exercises and uses margin notes to preview later chapters (light-cone narrowing, horizons, Ricci as volume change).

sections.title: Part III opener and chapter opening: why gravity rules the cosmos
sections.summary: A one-page Part III preface maps the arc: two toy universes here, possible constant-curvature geometries (ch16), filling them with matter (ch17), many models (ch18), and infinity and causal structure (ch19). The chapter opening then justifies cosmology as a gravitational problem: of the four interactions gravity is the feeblest, yet it is long range and never screened by opposite charges, so its effects add up over huge distances. It previews two themes: solvable models typically have spatial geometry that changes with time (cosmic evolution, unsettling to early relativists who expected a static cosmos), and many models begin or end in a singularity where classical field theory fails.
concepts: gravity as the dominant long-range interaction
key_moves: Compare gravity with the strong, weak and electromagnetic forces: range and sign, not strength, decide which force governs the largest scales.
Frame the solvable models as having time-dependent spatial metric components.
Flag singularities as a known difficulty to be handled later.

sections.title: The cosmological principle
sections.summary: States the programme: solve the field equation with Lambda for the entire matter content, i.e. find the metric at every event. A margin note fixes G = c = 1 for Part III and recommends the strategy of matching Einstein-tensor components to those of T and Lambda g. Another stresses the block-universe view: spacetime as a whole is fixed even though spatial metric components depend on t. The Copernican principle (our viewpoint is typical) motivates the cosmological principle of spatial homogeneity and isotropy. The authors immediately concede it fails on everyday, Solar-System and galactic scales, and Example 15.1 climbs a distance ladder (AU, light-year, parsec, kpc, Mpc) to show that lumpiness washes out only beyond roughly 100 Mpc. Cosmological models therefore apply only above that scale, with matter smeared (coarse-grained) into a uniform perfect fluid, dust if non-interacting.
concepts: Einstein field equation with cosmological constant
key_moves: Frame the goal of cosmology as determining the metric at every event from the total (smoothed) matter and Lambda content.
Distinguish homogeneity (same at every place) from isotropy (same in every direction).
Use deliberate counterexamples (sky versus ground, mountains versus valleys, Solar System versus intergalactic space) to show the principle is a large-scale statement.
Example 15.1: build the distance ladder and identify about 100 Mpc (3e24 m) as the scale where the Universe looks smooth.
Replace discrete galaxies by a continuous perfect fluid (coarse-graining), with a pixelated-screen analogy in a margin note.

sections.title: The Hubble flow
sections.summary: Introduces Hubble's law v = H0 r from redshift measurements, with H0 quoted as 70 km/s/Mpc, and reads it as expansion. It resolves the apparent special-position paradox by writing all positions as a(t) times their values at t0, so every pairwise separation scales the same way and every observer sees the same linear law; differentiating gives H(t) = a-dot/a, a parameter that in general varies with time. Physical coordinates r(t) are distinguished from comoving coordinates r(t0), in which galaxies sit still. The Hubble flow is the expansion-driven motion; proper (peculiar) motions such as orbital motion in clusters, or our motion that produces the CMB dipole, sit on top of it. Gravitationally bound systems such as the Solar System are governed by local interactions and do not expand.
concepts: CMB rest frame and dipole anisotropy
key_moves: Assume uniform rescaling r(t) = a(t) r(t0) with a(t0) = 1.
Subtract two position vectors so the origin choice cancels: r_ij(t) = a(t) r_ij(t0).
Differentiate to get v_ij = (a-dot/a) r_ij, so the Hubble law is the same for every galaxy and H = a-dot/a.
Define comoving coordinates (fixed labels) versus physical coordinates (stretched by a).
Separate Hubble flow from superposed proper motions; use the CMB dipole as evidence of our own motion.
Limit the theory to scales where local binding is irrelevant.

sections.title: Cosmic time
sections.summary: Builds the coordinate system for cosmology. A cosmic time t, which a margin note ties to any monotonically evolving scalar such as the radiation temperature, labels a stack of non-intersecting spacelike hypersurfaces that foliate spacetime; on each slice density, pressure and curvature are uniform and no direction is special. Observers moving relative to this system would see anisotropy, so it is singled out. Comoving observers ride with the cosmic fluid and their world lines pierce the slices. Example 15.2 argues that isotropy forces those world lines to be orthogonal to the slices, giving g_{0i}=0, e_0 = u and g_00 = -1, and shows that when g_{00,i} and g_{0i,0} vanish, Gamma^i_{00}=0 so particles at rest stay at rest. Weyl's postulate asserts a smooth, non-crossing bundle of timelike geodesics of fundamental observers whose proper time equals cosmic time. The section ends with the general comoving metric ds^2 = -dt^2 + a(t)^2 gamma_ij dx^i dx^j, credited to Robertson and Walker, with details deferred to ch16.
concepts: orthogonality of world lines to homogeneous slices
key_moves: Define time by a physical clock shared by all: a monotonic scalar field (e.g. CMB temperature), which forces all equivalent coordinate systems to agree on t.
Picture spacetime as a stack of sheets (homogeneity relates points on one sheet by an isometry at fixed t; isotropy is a rotation isometry fixing a point).
Argue that a tilt between world lines and slices would define a preferred spatial direction, contradicting isotropy.
Translate the geometry into metric conditions g_{0i}=0 and g_00=-1 and identify e_0 with the fluid four-velocity.
Use the geodesic equation: Gamma^i_{00}=0 means a particle at rest in these coordinates stays at rest.
State Weyl's postulate and identify cosmic time with the fundamental observers' proper time.
Write the general comoving metric with a(t) multiplying a time-independent spatial metric.

sections.title: Universe 0: an empty universe
sections.summary: The simplest model has no matter and no energy, so the Einstein tensor must vanish; since R is the trace of the Ricci tensor, Ricci-flatness suffices. Minkowski spacetime in Cartesian coordinates is comoving, fits the general form with a = 1 and flat gamma_ij, and has vanishing Riemann tensor, so it solves the problem; its slices are Euclidean and its geodesics are straight lines in proper time. Margin notes warn that Ricci-flat does not generally mean Riemann-flat, since positive and negative curvature contributions can cancel in the contraction (the Schwarzschild exterior is our example, not the book's), mention the iconic photo of Einstein writing R_ik = 0, and give the metric in spherical polars and in light-cone coordinates u = t - r, v = t + r for later use. The model is dismissed as unrealistic.
key_moves: Set T = 0 and note that R_mu nu = 0 implies G_mu nu = 0.
Check that Minkowski satisfies the comoving conditions and has zero Riemann tensor.
Write geodesics as x^mu = b^mu tau + c^mu.
Caution (margin): Ricci can vanish while tidal Riemann components do not; Ricci measures volume change.
Rewrite flat space in (u, v) null coordinates as a tool for later causal-structure chapters.

sections.title: Universe 1: flat and expanding
sections.summary: Takes flat spatial slices scaled by a(t) and calls the model de Sitter. Margin notes point out that a slice at fixed t is Euclidean space scaled by a(t0) and that radial light rays obey dt/dr = plus or minus a(t), so light cones drawn in comoving coordinates narrow as a grows. Although slices are flat, spacetime is curved. Example 15.3 reads off orthonormal-frame Riemann components ä/a and (ȧ/a)^2, builds the vielbein, and contracts carefully with eta to get R_00 = -3ä/a, R_ii = aä + 2ȧ^2 and R = 6(ä/a + ȧ^2/a^2). It then asks what source fits and tries pure vacuum energy, G = -Lambda g. Example 15.4 solves the 00 equation: 3ȧ^2/a^2 = Lambda, so a = exp(Ht) with H^2 = Lambda/3, an accelerating expansion that also satisfies the spatial equations. The line element is rewritten with this a(t), H is identified as a Hubble parameter, and Lambda is reinterpreted as a fluid with energy density Lambda/8pi and pressure -Lambda/8pi. A chapter summary closes the unit.
concepts: Riemann components of the flat expanding metric
Ricci scalar of the flat expanding metric
narrowing of light cones in comoving coordinates
key_moves: Write the flat expanding metric in Cartesian and spherical coordinates.
Note flat slices do not imply flat spacetime.
Choose e_0 = u and e_i-hat = e_i / a; vielbein components 1 and a.
Raise and lower in the local frame with eta, tracking two sign flips from pair swaps, to relate R^0_{i0i} to R^i_{0i0}.
Contract to R_00 = -3ä/a and R_ii = a ä + 2ȧ^2; take the trace to get R.
Pose the inverse problem: which T produces this geometry? Try pure Lambda.
Solve the first-order 00 equation for exponential a(t); check spatial components.
Match T_vac = -Lambda g / 8pi with perfect-fluid form to read off p = -rho.

sections.title: Exercises
sections.summary: Eight problems: a Milky Way star-count estimate; connection coefficients and Riemann tensor of de Sitter; the constant-curvature condition giving Lambda = R/4 and its check against the computed R; a 2D Chebyshev-net metric whose constant-curvature condition becomes the sine-Gordon equation; the vacuum energy density of the strong interaction and the absurdly small curvature radius it would imply; radial geodesics in de Sitter showing momenta decay as 1/a; a light signal whose comoving reach saturates, revealing an event horizon; and straight-line geodesics of massive particles in exponential de Sitter.
concepts: decay of peculiar momentum with expansion
key_moves: Push the full Christoffel and Riemann computation onto the reader.
Connect the Lambda-only model to maximal symmetry via R_mu nu = R g_mu nu / 4.
Preview horizons (ch19) and redshifting via simple integrals.

concepts.name: cosmology
concepts.definition: The study of the large-scale structure, origin and evolution of the Universe as a whole; in general relativity it means finding spacetime metrics that solve Einstein's equation for the smoothed-out total matter and energy content.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated as the most ambitious application of the field equation just built; framed as specifying the metric at every point of space and time.
prerequisites: Einstein field equation with cosmological constant

concepts.name: gravity as the dominant long-range interaction
concepts.definition: Although gravity is by far the weakest fundamental interaction, it has infinite range and (for ordinary matter) is always attractive, so contributions from all masses add without cancellation; electromagnetism, though also long range, is neutralized by balanced charges. Hence gravity controls cosmic dynamics.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening comparison of the four fundamental interactions, with a margin note listing them.

concepts.name: cosmic evolution
concepts.definition: The property of cosmological solutions that the spatial part of the metric depends on the time coordinate, so distances between comoving objects change in time.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced as the 'good news' of solvable models; noted that it troubled early relativists expecting a static cosmos. A margin note reconciles this with the block-universe view that spacetime as a whole is fixed.

concepts.name: spacetime singularity
concepts.definition: An event or boundary of spacetime where curvature or other quantities diverge and the smooth classical field description, and known physics, break down; many cosmological models begin (and some end) in one.
concepts.how_introduced: Named as the 'bad news' of cosmological models, with a promise that later chapters will show how to cope with them; reappears in Weyl's postulate as the only place fundamental world lines may meet.

concepts.name: Einstein field equation with cosmological constant
concepts.definition: The field equation of general relativity in geometrized units, in which the Einstein tensor plus Lambda times the metric equals eight pi times the energy-momentum tensor; it ties spacetime curvature to matter and energy, with Lambda a constant uniform contribution.
concepts.how_introduced: Restated at the start of the chapter as the equation cosmology must solve for all the matter in the Universe; a margin note describes the working strategy of matching components of G with those of kappa T and Lambda g.
concepts.notes: Sign convention: Lambda appears with a minus sign on the right, so positive Lambda acts like positive vacuum energy density.

concepts.name: Copernican principle
concepts.definition: The assumption that our location in the Universe is not privileged: observers elsewhere at the same cosmic epoch would see essentially the same Universe.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the first simplifying idea, with a biographical margin note on Copernicus, Gingerich's census of De Revolutionibus, and Bondi naming the modern principle; used later to answer whether Hubble's law puts us at the centre.

concepts.name: cosmological principle
concepts.definition: The assumption that, on sufficiently large scales, the Universe is spatially homogeneous and isotropic at each cosmic time.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in a highlighted box after the Copernican principle, then immediately challenged by everyday counterexamples and rescued by moving to scales above about 100 Mpc.
concepts.notes: Isotropy about every point implies homogeneity; the book states both separately.

concepts.name: spatial homogeneity
concepts.definition: Invariance of physical properties under translations within a spatial slice: every point of a constant-time hypersurface is equivalent to every other, related by an isometry that keeps t fixed.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as a bullet under the cosmological principle and later made geometric in Fig. 15.1 as points p and q on one hypersurface related by an isometry.

concepts.name: spatial isotropy
concepts.definition: Invariance under rotations about a point: at any event, a comoving observer finds no preferred spatial direction; geometrically, there is an isometry fixing the point and rotating any spatial direction into any other.
concepts.how_introduced: Bullet definition under the cosmological principle, then Fig. 15.2 shows two spacelike vectors at a point related by a rotation isometry; used to force world lines perpendicular to slices.

concepts.name: homogeneity scale and coarse-graining
concepts.definition: Averaging the discrete distribution of stars and galaxies over regions large enough (about 100 Mpc or more) that the averaged density is uniform, so matter can be modelled as a continuous fluid; the resulting models are not meant to describe smaller scales.
concepts.how_introduced: Arrived at via the distance ladder of Example 15.1 and a margin analogy with a grey screen made of pixels.

concepts.name: parsec
concepts.definition: The distance at which one astronomical unit subtends one arcsecond; 1 pc = 3.086e16 m, about 3.26 light-years. Kiloparsecs and megaparsecs measure galactic and cosmological distances.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 15.1 compares AU, light-year and parsec, with a margin note deriving the name from parallax of one arcsecond.

concepts.name: cosmological perfect fluid
concepts.definition: The coarse-grained matter content modelled as a perfect fluid of uniform density (and pressure) whose elements move with the cosmic expansion; with no internal interactions it is pressureless dust.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from ch12 as the natural stand-in for smoothed galaxies; allowed to move, expand and contract.

concepts.name: Hubble's law
concepts.definition: The observed linear relation between recession velocity and distance for galaxies, v = H0 r, valid at low redshift; interpreted as the uniform expansion of the Universe.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as an observational fact from redshifts, then derived kinematically from uniform scaling to show every galaxy sees the same law.
concepts.notes: The book writes it as an exact vector law; in relativity the linear velocity-distance relation is only a low-redshift statement.

concepts.name: Hubble parameter
concepts.definition: The fractional expansion rate H(t) = a-dot/a; its present value H0 is the Hubble constant, about 70 km/s per Mpc as quoted in the book. In the de Sitter model H is truly constant, equal to sqrt(Lambda/3).
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced with Hubble's law, then derived from the scale factor; a margin note warns that it is generally time-dependent. Reappears as the rate constant in the exponential solution.
concepts.notes: The book says Hubble's original value was nearly an order of magnitude too large (about 500 versus about 70 km/s/Mpc, i.e. roughly sevenfold).

concepts.name: scale factor
concepts.definition: A dimensionless function of cosmic time that multiplies all comoving separations to give physical separations; normalized so that a(t0) = 1 today.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the uniform stretch r(t) = a(t) r(t0) that makes Hubble's law origin-independent, then inserted into the general metric and solved for in Universe 1.

concepts.name: comoving coordinates
concepts.definition: Spatial coordinates attached to the cosmic fluid, so that galaxies without peculiar motion keep fixed coordinate labels while their physical separations grow with a(t); a particle at rest in them stays at rest.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined as r(t0) versus physical r(t) in the Hubble-flow discussion; a margin note gives the operational definition; Example 15.2 supplies the metric test Gamma^i_00 = 0.

concepts.name: physical coordinates
concepts.definition: Positions or separations measured at fixed cosmic time as actual distances, equal to the scale factor times the comoving values.
concepts.how_introduced: Paired with comoving coordinates when defining the Hubble flow.

concepts.name: Hubble flow
concepts.definition: The recession of objects caused purely by the growth of the scale factor, with all comoving labels fixed.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the second bullet of section 15.2 and contrasted with superposed proper motions.

concepts.name: peculiar motion
concepts.definition: Motion of an object relative to the local comoving frame, produced by local gravitational interactions, superposed on the Hubble flow.
concepts.how_introduced: Illustrated by galaxies bound in clusters and by the Earth's motion relative to the CMB.
concepts.notes: The book calls these 'proper motions'; in astronomy that term usually means angular motion on the sky, so 'peculiar velocity' is the standard cosmology name.

concepts.name: CMB rest frame and dipole anisotropy
concepts.definition: The cosmic microwave background is almost uniform over the sky, but our motion relative to the frame in which it is isotropic Doppler-shifts it into a small dipole pattern (slightly hotter ahead, cooler behind).
concepts.how_introduced: Given as an example of proper motion superposed on the Hubble flow; a margin note explains the CMB as relic radiation from recombination and says the frame is physically distinguished though not privileged by the laws of physics.

concepts.name: bound systems do not expand
concepts.definition: Gravitationally (or otherwise) bound systems such as planetary orbits, stars and galaxies are held together by local interactions; the cosmic scale factor does not stretch them, and the expansion description applies only on scales above the homogeneity scale.
concepts.how_introduced: A brief remark (with a joke about waistlines) that the Solar System ignores a(t), since local forces dominate and the cosmic curvature there is negligible.

concepts.name: cosmic time
concepts.definition: A global time coordinate t equal to the proper time of comoving fundamental observers, whose constant-t slices are the hypersurfaces on which the Universe is homogeneous and isotropic; operationally it can be read from any monotonically evolving scalar such as the background radiation temperature.
concepts.how_introduced: Built as the time a sensible astronomer would use; a margin note argues that defining t through a scalar S forces all equivalent systems to share the same t.

concepts.name: spacelike hypersurface
concepts.definition: A three-dimensional submanifold of spacetime obtained here by fixing t, whose tangent vectors are all spacelike; it represents space at one instant.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by holding one coordinate fixed; drawn as curled sheets in Figs. 15.1 and 15.3.

concepts.name: foliation of spacetime
concepts.definition: A decomposition of spacetime into a one-parameter family of non-intersecting hypersurfaces that together cover every event exactly once.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced with Fig. 15.1 as a stack of sheets labelled by cosmic time.

concepts.name: isometry
concepts.definition: A map of a (pseudo-)Riemannian space to itself that preserves all distances, i.e. leaves the metric unchanged; symmetries such as homogeneity (translations in a slice) and isotropy (rotations about a point) are isometries.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in the captions of Figs. 15.1 and 15.2 to make homogeneity and isotropy precise.

concepts.name: comoving observer
concepts.definition: An observer at rest in comoving coordinates, moving with the cosmic fluid; their world line is a timelike geodesic orthogonal to the homogeneous slices, their proper time is cosmic time, and they see the Universe as isotropic.
concepts.how_introduced: Described as going with the Hubble flow; drawn as arrows piercing sheets in Fig. 15.3; enshrined in Weyl's postulate.

concepts.name: orthogonality of world lines to homogeneous slices
concepts.definition: In a homogeneous, isotropic cosmology the four-velocity of the cosmic fluid is normal to the constant-time slices, so in comoving coordinates g_{0i} = 0 and, with t as proper time, g_00 = -1.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 15.2: a tilt between world lines and slices would pick out a spatial direction and contradict isotropy; the conclusion is written as three metric/basis conditions.

concepts.name: test for comoving coordinates
concepts.definition: If Gamma^i_{00} = 0, the geodesic equation shows that a particle initially at rest in the coordinates remains at rest, so the spatial coordinates are comoving; with g_{0i}=0 this holds when g_{00,i} = 0 and g_{0i,0} = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Given in Example 15.2 as a quick diagnostic and reused in margin notes to certify eqns 15.11 and 15.15.

concepts.name: Weyl's postulate
concepts.definition: The assumption that cosmic spacetime contains a family of fundamental observers whose world lines form a smooth congruence of timelike geodesics that never intersect, except possibly at an initial or final singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in a highlighted box after Example 15.2 with a margin note on Weyl and on the informal meaning of 'bundle'; illustrated by Fig. 15.3.

concepts.name: Robertson-Walker form of the metric
concepts.definition: The line element ds^2 = -dt^2 + a(t)^2 gamma_ij dx^i dx^j, in which homogeneity and isotropy restrict time dependence to an overall scale factor multiplying a fixed spatial metric of constant curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Assembled at the end of section 15.3 from g_00 = -1, g_0i = 0 and a homogeneous isotropic 3-metric; credited to Robertson and Walker and deferred to ch16 for the allowed gamma_ij.
prerequisites: orthogonality of world lines to homogeneous slices

concepts.name: spatial metric gamma_ij
concepts.definition: The time-independent metric on a constant-t slice (before scaling), a function of the spatial coordinates only, encoding the spatial curvature; for flat space it is the identity in Cartesian coordinates.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced when writing the metric of each slice as dsigma^2 = gamma_ij dx^i dx^j.

concepts.name: empty universe (Universe 0)
concepts.definition: The cosmological model with T_mu nu = 0 and Lambda = 0, satisfied by flat Minkowski spacetime written in comoving coordinates with a = 1 and Euclidean slices.
concepts.how_introduced: The first rung of the book's numbered ladder of model universes; checked against the general comoving form and dismissed as unrealistic.
concepts.notes: An empty universe can also be written with a(t) = t on hyperbolic slices (the Milne model); the book does not mention this here.

concepts.name: vacuum Einstein equation
concepts.definition: With no matter and no cosmological constant the field equation reduces to G_mu nu = 0, which is equivalent to R_mu nu = 0 because taking the trace forces R = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived for Universe 0 in one line from R = g^mu nu R_mu nu.

concepts.name: Ricci-flat versus Riemann-flat
concepts.definition: A vanishing Ricci tensor does not imply a vanishing Riemann tensor: tidal (Weyl) curvature can remain, as outside a star, while volume-changing curvature cancels.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin caution accompanying Universe 0: Ricci can vanish because positive and negative curvature parts cancel when it is formed, not because every Riemann component is zero; it adds that Ricci encodes the tendency of gravity to shrink volumes of matter and points ahead to ch35.
concepts.notes: The 'outside a star' illustration in the definition is the reviewer's, not the book's.

concepts.name: light-cone coordinates
aliases: u = t - r, v = t + r
concepts.definition: Coordinates u = t - r and v = t + r adapted to radial light rays, in which flat spacetime reads ds^2 = -du dv + (v - u)^2/4 dOmega^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note to Universe 0, flagged for use in later chapters on causal structure.

concepts.name: de Sitter model
concepts.definition: The spatially flat cosmology with metric ds^2 = -dt^2 + e^{2Ht}(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2), sourced only by a positive cosmological constant with H = sqrt(Lambda/3); it is a spacetime of constant curvature expanding exponentially.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a flat expanding metric with unspecified a(t), its curvature computed in Example 15.3, and its a(t) fixed in Example 15.4 by demanding a pure-Lambda source.
prerequisites: Ricci scalar of the flat expanding metric
concepts.notes: The flat coordinates cover only half of the full de Sitter hyperboloid; the book's name is applied before a(t) is determined, when strictly only the exponential case is de Sitter.

concepts.name: Riemann components of the flat expanding metric
aliases: curvature of a spatially flat FRW metric
concepts.definition: For ds^2 = -dt^2 + a^2 (flat 3-metric), the orthonormal-frame curvature has R^0_{i0i} = ä/a (time-space) and R^i_{jij} = (ȧ/a)^2 for i not equal to j (space-space), with no sums.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted in Example 15.3 with the derivation from Christoffel symbols deferred to Exercise 15.2.
formulas: R^{\hat i}{}_{\hat j\hat i\hat j} = (\dot a/a)^2

concepts.name: Ricci scalar of the flat expanding metric
concepts.definition: Contracting gives R_00 = -3ä/a, R_ii = aä + 2ȧ^2 (coordinate basis) and R = 6(ä/a + ȧ^2/a^2), the same in any frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Worked through in Example 15.3 by contracting in the orthonormal frame and transforming to coordinates with the vielbein.
prerequisites: Riemann components of the flat expanding metric

concepts.name: orthonormal frame and vielbein
concepts.definition: A basis e_mu-hat with e_mu-hat . e_nu-hat = eta_mu nu, related to the coordinate basis by vielbein components; here e_0-hat = u and e_i-hat = e_i / a, so (e_0)^0-hat = 1 and (e_i)^i-hat = a.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited from ch10 as practice: components are raised and lowered with eta in the hatted frame, then transformed back to coordinates.

concepts.name: cosmological constant as vacuum energy
concepts.definition: A term Lambda g_mu nu in the field equation that can be moved into the source as T_vac = -Lambda g / 8pi, i.e. a perfect fluid with uniform energy density rho = Lambda/8pi and pressure p = -rho in every frame.
concepts.how_introduced: After the curvature of the flat expanding metric is computed, the book asks what source could produce it and tries pure vacuum energy (no matter), which turns out to be consistent; at the end of 15.5 it is recast as a fluid by comparison with the vacuum tensor of ch13.
prerequisites: Einstein field equation with cosmological constant

concepts.name: exponential expansion
concepts.definition: Growth of the scale factor as e^{Ht} with constant H, so that ä > 0 and every comoving separation grows by the same factor in equal times.
concepts.how_introduced: Result of solving 3ȧ^2/a^2 = Lambda in Example 15.4; plotted in Fig. 15.4 and pictured as a flaring grid in Fig. 15.5.

concepts.name: negative pressure of vacuum energy
concepts.definition: Vacuum energy has pressure equal to minus its energy density; in general relativity pressure contributes to gravity through rho + 3p, so a component with p = -rho has net repulsive effect and accelerates expansion.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered at the end of section 15.5 by matching the vacuum tensor to the perfect-fluid form; the book's intuition is that such a medium, squeezed, tends to expand.
formulas: \ddot a/a = -\tfrac{4\pi}{3}(\rho+3p) \text{ (standard result, not in this chapter)}
concepts.notes: The rho + 3p explanation is the standard one and is not given in this chapter; see gaps_and_pitfalls.

concepts.name: narrowing of light cones in comoving coordinates
concepts.definition: Radial null rays in a flat expanding metric satisfy dt/dr = plus or minus a(t), so when drawn in comoving coordinates the light cones close up as a grows: light covers less comoving distance per unit time.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note to section 15.5, pointing ahead to ch25.

concepts.name: constant-curvature spacetime
concepts.definition: A spacetime whose curvature is fixed entirely by the Ricci scalar, with R_mu nu = (R/4) g_mu nu in four dimensions; de Sitter is an example, and for it Lambda = R/4.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted in the chapter summary for de Sitter and developed in Exercise 15.3; a 2D analogue in Exercise 15.4 leads to the sine-Gordon equation.
concepts.notes: R_mu nu proportional to g is strictly the Einstein-space condition; constant curvature additionally fixes the full Riemann tensor, which holds for de Sitter.

concepts.name: cosmological event horizon
concepts.definition: In an eternally accelerating universe the comoving distance that light emitted at a given time can ever reach is finite, so events beyond a certain distance can never be influenced by, or send signals to, a given observer.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 15.7 from the finite limit of the light-travel integral, pointing to ch19.
prerequisites: narrowing of light cones in comoving coordinates

concepts.name: decay of peculiar momentum with expansion
concepts.definition: A freely moving particle in an expanding universe loses momentum relative to comoving observers, with the physical speed-squared (spatial four-velocity) scaling as 1/a^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 15.6 via radial geodesics in de Sitter.

concepts.name: cosmological constant problem
concepts.definition: Taking zero-point energies of quantum fields at face value gives a vacuum energy density so large that the corresponding curvature radius of the universe would be absurdly tiny, in flagrant conflict with observation.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 15.5 asks for an order-of-magnitude estimate using the strong interaction's energy and length scales.

concepts.name: sine-Gordon equation
concepts.definition: The nonlinear wave equation theta_{,uv} = alpha sin theta; in geometry it expresses constant Gaussian curvature for a surface in Chebyshev-net coordinates.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 15.4 derives it from a constant-curvature condition on a 2D metric with angle function theta(u, v).

key_equations.name: Einstein field equation with Lambda
key_equations.meaning: The equation to be solved for the entire smoothed matter content of the Universe; geometry on the left, matter and cosmological constant on the right.
key_equations.symbols: R_mu nu Ricci tensor; R Ricci scalar; g metric; T energy-momentum tensor; Lambda cosmological constant; G = c = 1

key_equations.name: Parsec
key_equations.meaning: Conversion of the astronomer's distance unit; about 3.26 light-years.

key_equations.name: Hubble's law
key_equations.meaning: Recession velocity proportional to distance, with H0 quoted as 70 km/s/Mpc.
key_equations.symbols: v velocity; r position relative to us; H0 Hubble constant

key_equations.name: Uniform scaling
key_equations.meaning: All positions scale with a single time-dependent factor.

key_equations.name: Scaling of separations
key_equations.meaning: Separations between any two objects scale the same way, independent of the choice of origin.

key_equations.name: Relative velocity in uniform expansion
key_equations.latex: \vec v_{ij}(t) = \dot{\vec r}_{ij}(t) = \dot a(t)\,\vec r_{ij}(t_0) = \frac{\dot a(t)}{a(t)}\,\vec r_{ij}(t)
key_equations.meaning: Every pair recedes at a rate proportional to its current separation, so every observer sees a Hubble law.

key_equations.name: Hubble parameter
key_equations.meaning: Expansion rate as the logarithmic derivative of the scale factor; generally time dependent.

key_equations.name: Slices orthogonal to world lines
key_equations.meaning: No time-space cross terms in comoving coordinates, required by isotropy.
key_equations.symbols: e_0 timelike basis vector; e_i spatial basis vectors

key_equations.name: Time basis vector is the fluid velocity
key_equations.meaning: The comoving observer's four-velocity coincides with the coordinate time direction.

key_equations.name: Normalization of cosmic time
key_equations.meaning: Cosmic time equals the proper time of comoving observers.

key_equations.name: Comoving test via geodesic equation
key_equations.latex: \ddot x^\mu + \Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta}\dot x^\alpha\dot x^\beta = 0,\quad \Gamma^i_{00}=0 \Rightarrow \ddot x^i = 0 \text{ for a particle at rest}
key_equations.meaning: If Gamma^i_00 vanishes (guaranteed when g_00,i = g_0i,0 = 0) a particle at rest stays at rest, so the coordinates are comoving.
key_equations.symbols: Gamma connection coefficients; dots derivatives along the world line

key_equations.name: General comoving homogeneous-isotropic metric
key_equations.meaning: Robertson-Walker form: proper-time cosmic clock plus a fixed spatial geometry scaled by a(t).
key_equations.symbols: gamma_ij spatial metric depending only on x^i

key_equations.name: Empty-universe Einstein equation
key_equations.meaning: Field equation for Universe 0 with no matter, energy or Lambda; satisfied whenever R_mu nu = 0.

key_equations.name: Minkowski metric in spherical polars
key_equations.latex: \mathrm ds^2 = -\mathrm dt^2 + \mathrm dr^2 + r^2\left(\mathrm d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,\mathrm d\phi^2\right)
key_equations.meaning: Flat spacetime in polar coordinates (margin note).

key_equations.name: Minkowski metric in light-cone coordinates
key_equations.latex: \mathrm ds^2 = -\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv + \frac14(v-u)^2\left(\mathrm d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,\mathrm d\phi^2\right),\quad u=t-r,\ v=t+r
key_equations.meaning: Flat spacetime with radial null coordinates, prepared for causal-structure chapters (margin note).

key_equations.name: Universe 0 metric
key_equations.meaning: Minkowski spacetime in comoving Cartesian coordinates solves the empty-universe equation (Riemann tensor zero).

key_equations.name: Geodesics of Universe 0
key_equations.meaning: Free particles move on straight lines parametrized by proper time.
key_equations.symbols: b, c constant 4-vectors; tau proper time

key_equations.name: Spatially flat expanding metric
key_equations.latex: \mathrm ds^2 = -\mathrm dt^2 + a(t)^2\left(\mathrm dx^2+\mathrm dy^2+\mathrm dz^2\right) = -\mathrm dt^2 + a(t)^2\left[\mathrm dr^2 + r^2\left(\mathrm d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,\mathrm d\phi^2\right)\right]
key_equations.meaning: Universe 1 ansatz: flat slices stretched by a(t); spacetime is curved even though slices are flat.

key_equations.name: Null rays in flat expanding metric
key_equations.meaning: Radial light-ray slopes in comoving coordinates; cones narrow as a grows (margin note 22).

key_equations.name: Metric components of Universe 1
key_equations.meaning: Diagonal metric and inverse used in the curvature computation.

key_equations.name: Orthonormal Riemann components
key_equations.latex: R^{\hat0}{}_{\hat i\hat0\hat i} = \frac{\ddot a}{a},\qquad R^{\hat i}{}_{\hat j\hat i\hat j} = \left(\frac{\dot a}{a}\right)^2\quad(\text{no sum},\ i\neq j)
key_equations.meaning: Time-space curvature set by acceleration of expansion; space-space curvature set by the square of the expansion rate. The page render confirms the printed time-space entry is a-double-dot over a; the text export garbles it to a-dot over a.

key_equations.name: Vielbein components
key_equations.latex: (\boldsymbol e_0)^{\hat0}=1,\quad (\boldsymbol e_i)^{\hat i}=a,\quad (\boldsymbol e_{\hat0})^{0}=1,\quad (\boldsymbol e_{\hat i})^{i}=\frac1a
key_equations.meaning: Conversion factors between coordinate and orthonormal bases for the comoving observer (margin note 23).

key_equations.name: Ricci 00 component as a sum
key_equations.meaning: Contraction of Riemann over the first and third indices, written out explicitly.

key_equations.name: Index gymnastics with eta
key_equations.latex: \frac{\ddot a}{a} = -R_{\hat0\hat i\hat0\hat i} = -R_{\hat i\hat0\hat i\hat0} = -R^{\hat i}{}_{\hat0\hat i\hat0}
key_equations.meaning: Lowering 0 with eta_00 = -1 gives a sign; swapping within both index pairs gives two cancelling signs; raising a spatial index costs nothing.
key_equations.symbols: eta Minkowski metric in the local frame

key_equations.name: Orthonormal R_00
key_equations.meaning: Sum of three equal time-space contributions.

key_equations.name: Coordinate R_00
key_equations.meaning: Unchanged by the vielbein because (e_0)^0-hat = 1.

key_equations.name: Orthonormal R_ii
key_equations.latex: R_{\hat i\hat i} = R^{\hat0}{}_{\hat i\hat0\hat i} + \sum_{j\neq i}R^{\hat j}{}_{\hat i\hat j\hat i} = \frac{\ddot a}{a} + 2\left(\frac{\dot a}{a}\right)^2
key_equations.meaning: One time-space term plus two space-space terms (j = i contributes zero by antisymmetry).

key_equations.name: Coordinate R_ii
key_equations.latex: R_{ii} = (\boldsymbol e_i)^{\hat i}(\boldsymbol e_i)^{\hat i}R_{\hat i\hat i} = a^2R_{\hat i\hat i} = a\ddot a + 2\dot a^2
key_equations.meaning: Transforming back to coordinates multiplies by a^2.

key_equations.name: Ricci scalar of flat expanding metric
key_equations.latex: R = g^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu} = 3\frac{\ddot a}{a} + \frac{3}{a^2}\left(2\dot a^2 + a\ddot a\right) = 6\left(\frac{\ddot a}{a} + \frac{\dot a^2}{a^2}\right)
key_equations.meaning: Frame-independent curvature scalar for any spatially flat FRW metric.

key_equations.name: Einstein equation with vacuum energy only
key_equations.meaning: Source for Universe 1: no matter, only a cosmological constant.

key_equations.name: 00 component substituted
key_equations.meaning: Insert R_00 and R with g_00 = -1; the second-derivative terms cancel.

key_equations.name: Friedmann-type equation for pure Lambda
key_equations.meaning: First-order constraint: the expansion rate squared is fixed by the vacuum energy (special case of the Friedmann equation H^2 = 8 pi rho/3 with rho = Lambda/8pi).

key_equations.name: de Sitter scale factor
key_equations.meaning: Exponential, accelerating expansion with constant Hubble parameter; also satisfies the spatial equations.

key_equations.name: de Sitter line element (flat slicing)
key_equations.latex: \mathrm ds^2 = -\mathrm dt^2 + e^{2Ht}\left[\mathrm dr^2 + r^2\left(\mathrm d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,\mathrm d\phi^2\right)\right],\quad H = (\Lambda/3)^{1/2}
key_equations.meaning: Universe 1 geometry. The book prints -dt instead of -dt^2 here (typo corrected).

key_equations.name: Vacuum energy as a perfect fluid
key_equations.meaning: Comparing with the diagonal perfect-fluid components (rho, p, p, p) in flat spacetime gives negative pressure equal in size to the energy density.

key_equations.name: de Sitter connection coefficients (Exercise 15.2)
key_equations.meaning: Only nonzero Christoffel symbols of the flat expanding metric.

key_equations.name: Constant-curvature (Einstein space) condition
key_equations.meaning: Ricci proportional to metric in 3+1 dimensions; leads to Lambda = R/4 for de Sitter (Exercise 15.3).

key_equations.name: 2D Chebyshev-net metric (Exercise 15.4)
key_equations.meaning: General 2D line element with coordinate lines meeting at angle theta.

key_equations.name: Ricci scalar of the 2D metric
key_equations.meaning: Curvature from mixed second derivative of the net angle; follows from Riemann (15.36) and Ricci (15.37) components.

key_equations.name: Sine-Gordon equation
key_equations.meaning: Constant curvature K turns the curvature formula into sine-Gordon (alpha = -K in the book's sign convention, by our own calculation).

key_equations.name: Radial Lagrangian in de Sitter (Exercise 15.6)
key_equations.latex: L = \left[\left(\frac{\mathrm dt}{\mathrm d\tau}\right)^2 - a(t)^2\left(\frac{\mathrm dr}{\mathrm d\tau}\right)^2\right]^{1/2}
key_equations.meaning: Geodesic Lagrangian for radial motion; the reading copy garbles the second term as dt/dtau, the page shows dr/dtau.

key_equations.name: Time equation of radial geodesics
key_equations.meaning: Evolution of the time component of the four-velocity after eliminating dr/dtau.

key_equations.name: First integral
key_equations.meaning: Conserved quantity implying the physical momentum per unit mass falls as 1/a.

key_equations.name: Comoving reach of a light signal
key_equations.meaning: Comoving radius reached by light emitted at t_s by time t_r; bounded by e^{-Ht_s}/H as t_r grows, signalling an event horizon.
key_equations.symbols: t_s send time; t_r receive time

key_equations.name: de Sitter metric in Cartesian flat slicing
key_equations.latex: \mathrm ds^2 = -\mathrm dt^2 + e^{2Ht}\left(\mathrm dx^2+\mathrm dy^2+\mathrm dz^2\right)
key_equations.meaning: Starting point for showing massive-particle geodesics are straight lines (Exercise 15.8).

figures.label: Fig. 15.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Spacetime is sliced into a stack of spacelike hypersurfaces; homogeneity means any point p on a slice is equivalent to any other point q on it, the two being related by a distance-preserving map that leaves t unchanged.
figures.visual_description: Hand-drawn perspective sketch of three wavy, paper-like sheets stacked one above another with gaps between them, edges curling like pages. Light dotted shading gives texture. On the top sheet two black dots are labelled p (left) and q (right), joined by a curved arrow running from p to q. There are no axes; the vertical stacking stands for the time direction.
figures.what_it_teaches: Cosmic time labels slices; homogeneity is a symmetry acting within a slice (an isometry at fixed t), not a statement across times.

redesign.idea: 3D stack of translucent slices through a toy expanding universe filled with a random but statistically uniform scatter of galaxies; a draggable marker p on one slice can be moved to any q, and the local view (a small inset 'sky' from that point, averaged over a chosen smoothing radius) is shown to be statistically the same.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags p across a slice and adjusts a smoothing-radius slider; below about the homogeneity scale the inset sky changes from place to place, above it the inset becomes indistinguishable; a time slider moves between slices showing that density changes with t but not with position.

figures.label: Fig. 15.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Fluid world lines are perpendicular to the spatial slices; isotropy at a point P means the Universe looks the same along any two spatial directions e1 and e2, both of which must be orthogonal to the world-line tangent e0; a rotation isometry fixing P takes e1 into e2.
figures.visual_description: About eight thin, gently curved parallel lines rise from lower left to upper right like combed hair, representing world lines. On one line, near the centre, a dot labelled P has three short arrows: e0 points up along the line (tangent), e2 points to the right, and e1 points downward and slightly right. No slices are drawn, only the world lines and the local basis.
figures.what_it_teaches: Isotropy is a rotational symmetry about an event in the space orthogonal to the comoving observer's four-velocity; any preferred spatial direction, including a tilt of the slices, would break it.
concepts: orthogonality of world lines to homogeneous slices

redesign.idea: Spacetime diagram of a family of fluid world lines with an adjustable family of slices; at a selected event the learner sees e0 and a circle of spatial directions; tilting the slices relative to the world lines makes the circle of directions lopsided (a projected velocity arrow appears), visually showing a preferred direction.
redesign.interaction: Slider for the tilt angle between slices and world lines; rotating handle spins e1 toward e2 about P; a readout shows g_0i, which vanishes only when the tilt is zero.

figures.label: Fig. 15.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: The timelike geodesics of cosmic observers cross all the spacelike slices at right angles.
figures.visual_description: Three curved sheets stacked in perspective, similar to Fig. 15.1, pierced by a bundle of roughly a dozen upward-pointing arrows that start below the lowest sheet and pass through all three, fanning out slightly toward the top. Text labels read 'timelike geodesics' above the arrows and 'spacelike hypersurfaces' at the right with leader lines to the sheets.
figures.what_it_teaches: Weyl's postulate: a smooth, non-crossing congruence of fundamental-observer geodesics threads the foliation orthogonally; their proper time is cosmic time, and the slight fanning hints at expansion.

redesign.idea: Animated 3D view (two space dimensions plus time) of comoving world lines as glowing threads through expanding slices; the fan-out follows a chosen a(t), and a toggle adds a peculiar-velocity observer whose tilted world line crosses slices obliquely and whose local sky shows a dipole.
redesign.interaction: Choose a(t) (constant, power law, exponential); scrub time; click a thread to ride along and see isotropic sky, or launch a moving observer to see CMB-like dipole colouring.

figures.label: Fig. 15.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Plot of the scale factor against time in the de Sitter model.
figures.visual_description: A simple function plot: horizontal axis t with an arrow, vertical axis a(t) with an arrow, the vertical axis crossing about a third of the way along. A single smooth curve hugs the t axis far to the left (approaching zero but never reaching it), crosses the vertical axis at a small positive value, and rises ever more steeply to the upper right. No tick marks or numbers.
figures.what_it_teaches: Exponential growth: a never vanishes in the past (no Big Bang in these coordinates) and its slope and curvature both increase, i.e. accelerating expansion.

redesign.idea: Live plot of a(t) = exp(Ht) alongside H(t) and ä, with Lambda as the control; overlay alternative a(t) curves (empty, matter-like t^(2/3)) for later chapters, all normalized to a = 1 today with matching slope.
redesign.interaction: Slider for Lambda updates H = sqrt(Lambda/3), the curve, the doubling time ln2/H, and a flat readout that H stays constant while a-dot grows.

figures.label: Fig. 15.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Universe 1 has flat spatial slices whose scale factor grows exponentially in time.
figures.visual_description: Perspective drawing of a flared, block-like stack: a small flat square grid (four by four cells) at the bottom, a larger grid of the same four-by-four pattern part way up, and a much larger four-by-four grid on top. The side edges joining the grids curve outward more and more steeply, drawn with dashed and dotted lines. A column of small upward arrows at the left is labelled 'time'.
figures.what_it_teaches: Comoving grid cells keep their labels and count while their physical size grows; slices stay flat (square grids), and the outward-bending edges show the accelerating growth of a(t).

redesign.idea: Animated expanding lattice with galaxies pinned at grid nodes; each galaxy can be selected as 'home' to show that every node sees neighbours recede with v proportional to distance, and light pulses sent between nodes to show comoving reach saturating (horizon).
redesign.interaction: Play/scrub cosmic time; pick a home galaxy (Hubble diagram of velocities versus distance updates); emit a light pulse at time t_s and watch its comoving radius creep toward the finite limit exp(-H t_s)/H (the event horizon); toggle comoving versus physical view.

worked_examples.label: Example 15.1
worked_examples.problem: Place astronomical distances on a common ladder to find the scale at which the Universe starts to look homogeneous and isotropic.
worked_examples.method: Compare the AU, light-year and parsec (defined via one-arcsecond parallax); quote nearest-star distances, Milky Way size and star count, and the distance to Andromeda; then jump to 100 Mpc and express it in metres and in AU.
worked_examples.key_insight: Up to Mpc scales matter is lumpy; only above roughly 100 Mpc does the cosmological principle hold, which fixes the domain of validity of every model in Part III.
worked_examples.result: 1 pc = 3.086e16 m ~ 3.26 ly; Proxima 1.3 pc, Sirius 2.7 pc; ~1e11 stars in a disc of radius ~25 kpc, thickness ~0.3 kpc; Andromeda ~770 kpc; 100 Mpc ~ 3e24 m, over 13 orders of magnitude beyond 1 AU.

worked_examples.problem: Show that Hubble's law does not single out our location.
worked_examples.method: Assume all positions scale as a(t) r(t0); form separation vectors so the origin cancels; differentiate in time.
worked_examples.key_insight: Uniform scaling automatically gives a linear velocity-distance law about every point, so the law is compatible with the Copernican principle and defines H = a-dot/a.

worked_examples.problem: Show that a cosmic time defined by a monotonic physical scalar must be shared by all equivalent coordinate systems (margin note 14).
worked_examples.method: Let S (for example the background temperature) decrease monotonically and define t through S; since S is a scalar its value at an event is coordinate independent, so S(t) = S(t') forces t = t'.
worked_examples.key_insight: A universal clock can be tied to a physical field that evolves in the same way everywhere on a homogeneous slice.
worked_examples.result: t = t' for all cosmic-standard systems.

worked_examples.label: Example 15.2
worked_examples.problem: Turn homogeneity and isotropy into conditions on the metric of comoving coordinates, and give a test that coordinates are comoving.
worked_examples.method: Argue that fluid world lines must be orthogonal to the homogeneous slices, else a preferred direction appears; express this as dot products of basis vectors; then use the geodesic equation to show Gamma^i_00 = 0 keeps resting particles at rest and relate this to vanishing g_00,i and g_0i,0.
worked_examples.key_insight: Symmetry arguments fix g_0i = 0 and g_00 = -1 before any field equation is solved, leaving only the spatial part to be determined.
worked_examples.result: g_0i = 0, e_0 = u, g_00 = -1; comoving if g_00,i = g_0i,0 = 0.
concepts: orthogonality of world lines to homogeneous slices

worked_examples.problem: Find a cosmological solution for a universe with no matter, energy or cosmological constant (Universe 0).
worked_examples.method: Reduce G = 0 to R_mu nu = 0 using the trace; test Minkowski in comoving Cartesian coordinates against eqn 15.11 and note its Riemann tensor vanishes; write its geodesics.
worked_examples.key_insight: The trivial solution already fits the cosmological framework (a = 1, flat gamma), which calibrates the formalism before adding content.
worked_examples.result: ds^2 = -dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2; geodesics x^mu = b^mu tau + c^mu.

worked_examples.label: Example 15.3
worked_examples.problem: Compute the Ricci tensor and Ricci scalar of the spatially flat expanding metric using the orthonormal frame.
worked_examples.method: Write the metric and inverse; quote orthonormal Riemann components; set up the vielbein e_0-hat = u, e_i-hat = e_i/a; contract to R_00-hat with careful sign tracking via eta (one sign for lowering 0, two cancelling signs from pair swaps); contract R_ii-hat from one time-space and two space-space terms; transform back with vielbein factors 1 and a^2; take the trace with g^mu nu.
worked_examples.key_insight: Flat spatial slices do not mean flat spacetime: ä controls time-space curvature and ȧ^2 controls space-space curvature, and the Ricci scalar is frame independent.
concepts: Riemann components of the flat expanding metric
Ricci scalar of the flat expanding metric

worked_examples.label: Example 15.4
worked_examples.problem: Determine a(t) when the only source is a cosmological constant.
worked_examples.method: Substitute R_00 and R into the 00 component of G = -Lambda g; the ä terms cancel leaving a first-order ODE for a; integrate to an exponential; state that spatial components also check.
worked_examples.key_insight: With pure vacuum energy the expansion rate is fixed, H^2 = Lambda/3, so growth is exponential and accelerating. Our own check of the ii equation: aä + 2ȧ^2 - 3a^2(ä/a + ȧ^2/a^2) = -2aä - ȧ^2 = -3H^2 a^2 = -Lambda a^2, consistent.

worked_examples.problem: Interpret the cosmological constant as a material source.
worked_examples.method: Move Lambda g to the right-hand side as T_vac = -Lambda g/8pi (from ch13) and compare with the perfect-fluid components (rho, p, p, p) in flat spacetime.
worked_examples.key_insight: Vacuum energy behaves as a fluid with positive density and equal and opposite pressure, the property responsible for accelerated expansion.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A uniform grey patch on a screen that turns out, under a magnifier, to be a mosaic of tiny dots
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Margin note: the Universe looks smooth only when you step back far enough; close up (below ~100 Mpc) the pixels are galaxies and stars.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Screen pixels are regularly arranged and identical; galaxies cluster into filaments and voids with structure on many scales, so smoothness emerges statistically rather than exactly.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Zoom slider over a simulated galaxy distribution with a density-variance meter that drops toward zero as the averaging window approaches 100 Mpc.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Looking up (sky) versus down (ground), or walking from mountains to valleys
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Deliberate counterexamples showing the principle is obviously false locally, motivating the need to specify a scale.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only shows failure; does not quantify at what scale isotropy is restored.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Stack of curled paper sheets pierced by arrows
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Figs. 15.1 and 15.3 depict slices of constant cosmic time as sheets and fundamental observers as arrows crossing them.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Paper sheets are two-dimensional and embedded in 3D space; real slices are 3D, and their curvature in the picture has no direct meaning. Spacing between sheets does not show proper time.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Rotatable 3D stack with adjustable spacing tied to a(t), and threads that can be tilted to show what breaks isotropy.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Grid lines drawn on an expanding block (grid cells same in number, larger in size)
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Fig. 15.5 shows flat slices whose four-by-four grid enlarges with time while labels stay put.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The picture has an edge and an outside; the model universe has neither, and nothing expands 'into' anything.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Toggle between comoving and physical views of the same grid, with galaxies pinned at nodes.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A medium with negative pressure which, when squeezed, wants to expand
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Closing intuition for why positive Lambda leads to extra expansion.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Misleading if taken literally: uniform pressure exerts no net force, and a medium with negative pressure behaves like tension (it pulls inward). The real GR reason is that pressure itself gravitates via rho + 3p, which is negative for p = -rho.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Acceleration equation widget: sliders for rho and p (or w = p/rho) showing the sign of ä flip at w = -1/3.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Einstein's second most famous equation after E = mc^2: the blackboard 'R_ik = 0?'
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Light cultural aside anchoring the vacuum equation in memory.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Since every galaxy recedes from us, we must be at the centre of the expansion.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Uniform scaling gives the same linear velocity-distance law about every point; separations r_i - r_j scale with a(t) regardless of origin.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Explosion pictures have a centre, and we naturally measure from ourselves.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The cosmological principle claims the Universe is uniform everywhere, which is plainly false.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is a statement about averages over scales above roughly 100 Mpc; below that the Universe is lumpy and the models are not intended to apply.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Everyday experience and astronomy up to galaxy clusters are strongly inhomogeneous.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Cosmic expansion stretches the Solar System, atoms, rulers and people.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Bound systems are held by local forces and do not follow the Hubble flow; the expansion description applies only on very large scales.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: 'Space itself expands' suggests every length grows.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The CMB rest frame is a privileged frame that violates relativity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is physically distinguished by the matter content (the radiation is isotropic there), but the laws of physics are identical in all inertial frames.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Having a measurable absolute velocity (from the CMB dipole) sounds like an ether frame.
concepts: CMB rest frame and dipole anisotropy

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Hubble's 'constant' is the same at all times.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: H(t) = a-dot/a generally changes in time; it is constant only in special models such as de Sitter.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It is called a constant and quoted as a single number.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: If the Ricci tensor vanishes, spacetime is flat.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Ricci-flat only means volume-changing curvature cancels; tidal curvature (Riemann/Weyl) can remain, as in Schwarzschild. In Universe 0 the Riemann tensor happens to vanish too.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: R_mu nu = 0 is called the vacuum equation and Minkowski is the first solution met.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: If space is flat, spacetime is flat.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The de Sitter slices are Euclidean yet spacetime has nonzero curvature (R = 12H^2); time-space curvature comes from ä and space-space curvature from ȧ^2.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: 'Flat universe' in popular cosmology refers to spatial flatness and is easily confused with no curvature at all.
concepts: Riemann components of the flat expanding metric

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: An empty universe must be static, and any expanding universe must contain matter.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Universe 1 contains no matter at all, only vacuum energy, and yet expands exponentially; even an empty universe can be described with expanding coordinates (Milne).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian intuition ties dynamics to masses.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Negative pressure pushes things apart like a compressed gas.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Negative pressure is tension; its effect on expansion is gravitational, through the rho + 3p source term, which is negative when p = -rho.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book's own 'if squeezed, must expand' phrasing and everyday association of pressure with pushing.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Galaxies recede because they move through space away from each other.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In comoving coordinates galaxies are at rest; separation grows because the metric's scale factor grows, with peculiar motions as small additions.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Velocity language (v = H r) and Doppler intuition.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: An exponentially expanding universe must start in a Big Bang singularity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: a = e^{Ht} is positive for all t and never reaches zero; de Sitter has no initial singularity, though the flat coordinates cover only part of the full spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter opening stresses that many models begin in a singularity.

thought_experiments.name: Zooming out from a grain of sand to 100 Mpc
thought_experiments.setup: Start on Earth and repeatedly enlarge the field of view: Solar System, nearest stars, Galaxy, Local Group, then boxes of hundreds of megaparsecs, asking at each step whether the view is homogeneous and isotropic.
thought_experiments.lesson: Homogeneity and isotropy are scale-dependent statistical properties that emerge only on the largest scales.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Powers-of-ten zoom with a live histogram of density fluctuations in the current window.

thought_experiments.name: Every galaxy as its own centre
thought_experiments.setup: Lay out galaxies on a uniformly stretching lattice and compare the Hubble diagram measured from two different galaxies.
thought_experiments.lesson: Uniform expansion produces identical linear laws for all observers; no centre is required.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Click any galaxy to recentre; overlay both Hubble diagrams to show they coincide.

thought_experiments.name: Speeding spacecraft in the cosmic frame
thought_experiments.setup: An observer travels at high speed relative to the local comoving observers and looks at the sky.
thought_experiments.lesson: Isotropy holds only for comoving observers; the moving observer sees a dipole, which singles out the cosmic standard frame.
concepts: CMB rest frame and dipole anisotropy
thought_experiments.app_idea: Velocity slider that colours an all-sky map with the relativistic Doppler temperature pattern T/(gamma(1 - beta cos theta)).

thought_experiments.name: Tilted slices
thought_experiments.setup: Imagine the constant-time slices were not orthogonal to the fluid world lines.
thought_experiments.lesson: The fluid would appear to flow in a particular direction within each slice, violating isotropy; hence g_0i = 0.
concepts: orthogonality of world lines to homogeneous slices
thought_experiments.app_idea: Tilt control on a 1+1 spacetime diagram showing the resulting in-slice drift velocity.

thought_experiments.name: Racing a light pulse across de Sitter
thought_experiments.setup: Emit a light signal at time t_s and follow its comoving distance as the universe expands exponentially (Exercise 15.7).
thought_experiments.lesson: The comoving reach saturates at e^{-Ht_s}/H: some regions can never be reached, an event horizon.
concepts: narrowing of light cones in comoving coordinates
thought_experiments.app_idea: Comoving spacetime diagram with narrowing light cones and an asymptote line for the horizon.

historical_notes.event: Copernicus's heliocentric De Revolutionibus displaced Earth from the centre; Koestler called it an unread flop, Gingerich refuted this by surveying surviving copies; Bondi later named the cosmological Copernican principle.
historical_notes.significance: Roots the modern no-special-place assumption in the history of astronomy.

historical_notes.event: Found the linear velocity-distance relation from galaxy redshifts; the book notes his first value of H0 was nearly an order of magnitude above the modern one (historically about 500 km/s/Mpc, some seven times larger; that figure is our addition).
historical_notes.significance: Observational basis for an expanding universe and for introducing a(t).

historical_notes.event: Formulated the postulate that fundamental observers form a smooth non-crossing family of timelike geodesics.
historical_notes.significance: Supplies the preferred observers and cosmic time on which cosmological metrics are built.

historical_notes.event: Derived the general form of homogeneous isotropic metrics by symmetry (kinematic) arguments.
historical_notes.significance: The metric form 15.11 used throughout Part III.

historical_notes.event: Iconic photograph of Einstein at a blackboard with 'R_ik = 0?' written on it.
historical_notes.significance: Cultural anchor for the vacuum field equation.

historical_notes.event: Gave his name to the vacuum-energy-dominated expanding model (Universe 1).
historical_notes.significance: First non-trivial cosmological solution in the book; revisited in ch18-19.

historical_notes.event: Early relativists expected an unchanging, static universe and were uneasy with time-dependent solutions.
historical_notes.significance: Explains the historical resistance to cosmic evolution and the original motivation for Lambda.

applications_and_observations.details: Distances from the AU up to the homogeneity scale, used to justify coarse-graining.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 1 AU = 1.496e11 m; 1 ly ~ 9.46e15 m (>60,000 AU); 1 pc = 3.086e16 m = 3.26 ly; Proxima 1.3 pc; Sirius 2.7 pc; Andromeda ~770 kpc; 100 Mpc ~ 3e24 m.

applications_and_observations.details: Disc galaxy with typical star spacing of order a parsec.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: ~1e11 stars; disc radius ~25 kpc; thickness ~0.3 kpc. Our own check for Exercise 15.1: volume pi(25e3 pc)^2(300 pc) ~ 6e11 pc^3, so ~1e11-1e12 stars at one per pc^3.

applications_and_observations.details: Redshifts of emission lines show recession velocity proportional to distance.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: H0 = 70 km/s/Mpc as quoted (book claims ~10% accuracy). Our estimate: Hubble time 1/H0 ~ 14 Gyr; Hubble length c/H0 ~ 4.3 Gpc. Current measurements disagree at the ~8% level (about 67 vs 73 km/s/Mpc, the 'Hubble tension'), post-dating the book.

applications_and_observations.details: The microwave background is nearly isotropic but shows a dipole due to our motion relative to its rest frame, with an annual modulation from Earth's orbit and a net motion of the Local Group toward Hydra.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Not given in the book. Standard values: dipole amplitude ~3.4 mK on T ~ 2.725 K, corresponding to ~370 km/s for the Solar System.

applications_and_observations.topic: Vacuum energy from the strong interaction
applications_and_observations.details: Exercise 15.5: treat zero-point energy at nuclear scales as real vacuum energy and estimate the resulting curvature radius.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Inputs 1 GeV over 1e-15 m. Our estimate: energy density ~1.6e35 J/m^3 (mass density ~2e18 kg/m^3); c/H with H^2 = 8 pi G rho/3 gives a curvature radius of order 10 km, versus an observable universe of order 1e26 m.

applications_and_observations.details: The de Sitter model describes the late-time fate of a universe dominated by a positive cosmological constant, consistent with the observed acceleration of cosmic expansion; the book does not discuss the observations here.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our note: observed Lambda-energy fraction ~0.7 of the critical density; not in this chapter.

notation_and_conventions.convention: G = c = 1 throughout Part III unless stated.
(-,+,+,+): g_00 = -1 for comoving time, eta_00 = -1 in orthonormal frames.
Field equation written G_mu nu = 8 pi T_mu nu - Lambda g_mu nu, so T_vac = -Lambda g / 8 pi and positive Lambda means positive vacuum energy density.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Equivalent to the common G + Lambda g = 8 pi T.

notation_and_conventions.convention: a(t0) = 1 at the present time t0; a is dimensionless.
r(t) denotes physical coordinates and r(t0) comoving coordinates; r_ij = r_i - r_j is a separation.
Used for motion relative to the Hubble flow.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Standard cosmology term is peculiar velocity; astronomers reserve proper motion for angular motion on the sky.

notation_and_conventions.convention: gamma_ij for the unscaled 3-metric of slices, dsigma^2 for its line element.
Hats mark orthonormal-frame components; vielbein components written (e_mu)^nu-hat and (e_mu-hat)^nu.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Summation temporarily suspended in eqns 15.19-15.26; sums written explicitly.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Ricci formed by contracting first and third indices: R_mu nu = R^alpha_{mu alpha nu}; orthonormal component R^0_{i0i} = ä/a is positive in this convention.
Dot = d/dt (cosmic time) for a(t); comma = partial derivative, e.g. g_00,i and theta_,uv.
notation_and_conventions.notes: In the geodesic equation the dot means d/dtau.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Universe 0 (empty, Minkowski) and Universe 1 (flat, de Sitter); numbering continues in ch18.

margin_notes.summary: Part III opening page: gravity is now turned on the origin and fate of the Universe; roadmap of ch15 (ideas and two toy models), ch16 (homogeneous isotropic constant-curvature geometries; the page misprints 'isotopic'), ch17 (adding matter), ch18 (model universes) and ch19 (infinity and spacetime geometry).

Two chapter epigraphs: William Blake's lines about seeing a world in a grain of sand and eternity in an hour, and Thomas Carlyle's remark that the Universe is bigger than he is and people ought to be more modest; they set the tone of scale and humility for the cosmology part.
Lists the other three fundamental interactions alongside gravity.
Reminds the reader that Part III uses G = c = 1.
Strategy for Part III: solve G = kappa T - Lambda g by matching components of the geometry side with those of the matter and Lambda terms.
Block-universe remark: spacetime as a whole is fixed once solved, which is compatible with spatial metric components depending on t.
Biographical and bibliographic note on Copernicus, the 'book nobody read' controversy (Koestler versus Gingerich), and Bondi naming the Copernican principle.
Defines the parsec via a one-arcsecond parallax of one AU and explains the name.
Pixelated grey screen analogy for coarse-graining the Universe.
Position r can be thought of as the distance from Earth at the origin.
