Hubble biography; his first H0 was nearly ten times the modern value; the value is now known to about 10 per cent; warning that H varies in time and will be called the Hubble parameter H(t).
Working definition of comoving coordinates: a particle at rest stays at rest as coordinate time passes.
Explains the CMB as relic radiation from recombination, the physically special but not law-privileged CMB frame, and the dipole from Earth's orbit, Solar System and Local Group motion toward Hydra.
Jokes that the expansion of the Universe cannot be blamed for expanding waistlines, and that 'minuscule' here means under 100 Mpc.
Defines cosmic standard time through a monotonically changing scalar (e.g. radiation temperature) and argues all equivalent coordinate systems must share it.
Weyl biography; smoothness in Weyl's postulate justifies classical field theory; 'bundle' has a technical meaning explored in Appendix C.
For flat space gamma_ij is the identity; check that eqn 15.11 is comoving since g_0i,0 = g_00,i = 0.
Robertson and Walker biographical dates.
Caution that Ricci-flat does not force Riemann-flat; Ricci describes volume contraction (ch35); the iconic 'R_ik = 0?' blackboard photograph.
Minkowski metric in spherical polars and in light-cone coordinates u, v, to be used in coming chapters.
De Sitter biography; a geometric description of this spacetime is left to the ch18 exercises.
A fixed-t slice of Universe 1 is flat space rescaled by a; radial light rays obey dt/dr = plus or minus a(t), so light cones narrow as a grows (developed in ch25).
Derives the vielbein for the comoving observer from u^0 = 1 and e_i-hat = e_i / a.

using Ricci proportional to g to relate Lambda and R
curvature of a general 2D metric in Chebyshev-net form
estimating vacuum energy density and the implied curvature radius
deriving geodesic equations from a Lagrangian and finding first integrals
integrating null geodesics in an expanding universe to find horizons
showing straight-line geodesics in de Sitter coordinates

notable.summary: Use a parsec-scale star spacing and the quoted size of the Galactic disc to estimate the number of stars to the nearest power of ten.
notable.why_notable: Quick sanity check linking the distance ladder to the quoted 1e11 stars.

notable.summary: Derive the nonzero connection coefficients of the flat expanding metric and then its full Riemann tensor.
notable.why_notable: Fills the step that Example 15.3 skips; learners should reproduce eqn 15.19 by a coordinate route.

notable.summary: Treat de Sitter as a constant-curvature spacetime with Ricci equal to R g/4, find the Einstein tensor, deduce Lambda = R/4, and check against R = 6(ä/a + ȧ^2/a^2).
notable.why_notable: Shows that the Lambda-only solution is forced by maximal symmetry; the check gives R = 12H^2 = 4 Lambda.

notable.summary: For a 2D metric whose coordinate lines meet at a variable angle, compute Riemann, Ricci and scalar curvature and show that constant curvature turns into the sine-Gordon equation.
skills: link between geometry and nonlinear field equations
notable.why_notable: Surprising bridge from curvature to a famous soliton equation; note the metric is Riemannian, not Lorentzian, despite being called a spacetime.

notable.summary: Estimate the energy density associated with strong-interaction zero-point energy and the curvature radius a universe with that density would have, and comment.
notable.why_notable: A hands-on encounter with the cosmological constant problem: the answer is of order kilometres.

notable.summary: From the radial geodesic Lagrangian in de Sitter derive the time equation, verify a first integral, and use normalization of the four-velocity to show the spatial velocity squared falls as 1/a^2.
notable.why_notable: Demonstrates that expansion drains peculiar momentum, the particle analogue of cosmological redshift.

notable.summary: Follow a light signal from the origin in de Sitter to find its comoving reach as a function of send and receive times, and argue that a maximum distance exists.
notable.why_notable: First appearance of a cosmological event horizon, previewing ch19.

notable.summary: Show that in exponential de Sitter coordinates the geodesics of massive particles follow straight lines.
notable.why_notable: Clarifies what free motion looks like in comoving coordinates (spatial paths are straight, while speed decays).

difficulty.notes: Sections 15.1-15.2 are gentle and largely verbal with simple algebra. Section 15.3 is conceptually dense (foliation, isometries, Weyl's postulate, orthogonality argument) but light on computation and somewhat hand-waving. Example 15.3 is the hardest part: curvature components are quoted rather than derived, and the orthonormal-frame sign bookkeeping with eta and the vielbein demands comfort with ch10-11; index notation in 15.25 is loose. Example 15.4 is easy once R is in hand. The negative-pressure interpretation is intuitive but physically imprecise. A few printed slips (missing square on dt in 15.32 and on a(t0) in margin note 22) can confuse careful readers.

cross_references.target: Owen Gingerich, The Book Nobody Read
cross_references.reason: Census of surviving copies of De Revolutionibus, cited in the Copernicus margin note.

teaching_gems.gem: Derive Hubble's law from uniform scaling of separation vectors so that the origin cancels, instead of quoting it as an observation only.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns an apparently anthropocentric fact into a one-line consequence of a single function a(t), and naturally defines H = a-dot/a.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Stretchable 2D galaxy lattice: learner picks any galaxy as origin and watches the velocity-distance scatter plot remain a straight line of the same slope.

teaching_gems.gem: Admit that the cosmological principle is false in daily life, then climb a distance ladder until it becomes true.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Builds trust by confronting the obvious objection and gives the model a clear domain of validity (~100 Mpc).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Powers-of-ten zoom with a fluctuation meter (rms density contrast in the viewing box) falling toward zero near 100 Mpc.

teaching_gems.gem: Show slices and fundamental observers as a stack of sheets threaded by arrows before writing any metric component.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives a concrete geometric picture of cosmic time, homogeneity (within a sheet) and Weyl's postulate (threads never cross).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Rotatable 3D foliation with threads; tilting threads or letting them cross triggers warnings about broken isotropy or Weyl's postulate.

teaching_gems.gem: Use isotropy to kill metric cross terms: a tilt between world lines and slices would reveal a direction.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Converts a symmetry principle directly into g_0i = 0, teaching how symmetry constrains the metric before dynamics.
teaching_gems.app_idea: 1+1 diagram with a tilt slider; readouts show the induced in-slice velocity and the nonzero g_0t term.

teaching_gems.gem: Give a quick practical test for comoving coordinates: Gamma^i_00 = 0, guaranteed by g_00,i = g_0i,0 = 0.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Links an abstract coordinate property to the behaviour of a dropped test particle via the geodesic equation.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Metric playground: learner edits g_00 and g_0i functions and releases a particle at rest to see whether it drifts.

teaching_gems.gem: Ladder of numbered toy universes starting with an empty one that is secretly Minkowski space.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Calibrates the formalism on a known answer, then adds exactly one ingredient (Lambda) to get genuine dynamics.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Universe selector (0, 1, later matter and radiation) that swaps metric, a(t) plot, curvature readouts and source content side by side.

teaching_gems.gem: Flat slices but curved spacetime: ä sets time-space curvature and ȧ^2 sets space-space curvature.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Breaks the common identification of spatial flatness with no curvature and gives each Riemann component a physical handle.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Choose any a(t) curve; live panels show R^0_{i0i} = ä/a, R^i_{jij} = (ȧ/a)^2 and R, highlighting that exponential a gives constant values.

teaching_gems.gem: Invert the problem: compute curvature first, then ask which source fits, discovering that pure vacuum energy works.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows the 'guess metric, compute G, read off T' recipe used throughout Part III and makes Lambda feel discovered rather than imposed.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Guess-the-source game: learner adjusts a(t) family parameters until the implied rho and p satisfy p = -rho, landing on exponential growth.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eqn 15.32 is printed with -dt instead of -dt^2.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A careful reader may think the metric is inconsistent or dimensionally wrong.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write ds^2 = -dt^2 + e^{2Ht}[...] and note the typo.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Margin note 22 writes the fixed-time slice metric as a(t0)(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2); it should be a(t0)^2.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion about whether lengths scale with a or a^2.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Emphasize that distances scale with a and the metric with a^2.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The negative-pressure explanation ('if squeezed, must expand') is physically loose; uniform pressure exerts no force and negative pressure is tension. The actual reason is that pressure gravitates via rho + 3p in the acceleration equation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners form a wrong mechanical picture of dark energy and struggle later with the Friedmann acceleration equation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Preview ä/a = -(4 pi/3)(rho + 3p) and show that p = -rho gives ä/a = (8 pi/3) rho > 0, i.e. H^2 = Lambda/3 consistent with Example 15.4.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The model is named de Sitter before a(t) is determined; only the exponential case is de Sitter, and the flat slicing covers only half of the full de Sitter hyperboloid.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think any flat expanding universe is de Sitter, or that flat-slicing de Sitter is the whole spacetime.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Call the ansatz a spatially flat FRW metric and reserve 'de Sitter' for a = e^{Ht}; mention the hyperboloid picture (ch18).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Orthonormal Riemann components (15.19) are quoted without derivation, and index notation in 15.25 (sum j = 1 to 2, 'R^mu_{mu mu mu} = 0') is sloppy.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Novices cannot reproduce the result and may misread which components vanish.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Derive Christoffels (Exercise 15.2) first, or give a short coordinate derivation; write the sum as over j != i and note R^i_{iii} = 0 by antisymmetry.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Hubble's law is given as an exact vector relation with no mention that linearity holds only at low redshift and that recession 'velocities' can exceed c at large distance.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Later confusion over superluminal recession and over which distance and velocity are meant.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State v = H d exactly for proper distance and its rate of change at fixed cosmic time, and explain the observational version is only linear at small z.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: H0 = 70 km/s/Mpc 'to within about 10%' is dated; measurements now cluster near 67 (CMB) and 73 (distance ladder) km/s/Mpc.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Outdated sense of the precision and tension in cosmology.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present H0 with current values and a brief mention of the Hubble tension.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The orthogonality argument (Example 15.2) and the statement that the conditions for comoving coordinates 'are met' are asserted rather than shown; the cosmic-time argument in margin note 14 is terse.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may not see why g_0i = 0 follows and what exactly is being checked.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show explicitly that a nonzero shift vector in a slice defines a direction; compute Gamma^i_00 for eqn 15.11 in one line.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 15.4 calls a positive-definite 2D metric a 'spacetime'.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Describe it as a 2D surface (Chebyshev net) and note the Lorentzian analogue separately.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Book uses 'proper motion' for peculiar velocity and does not mention the Milne form of the empty universe.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Terminology clashes with astronomy texts; misses the lesson that an empty universe can look expanding in suitable coordinates.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Introduce 'peculiar velocity' and show Minkowski in Milne coordinates as an optional aside.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The claim that the de Sitter spacetime has constant curvature (summary) is not demonstrated in the text, only in Exercise 15.3.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Point out that with a = e^{Ht} all orthonormal Riemann components equal H^2, making constant curvature immediate.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: When reading vacuum energy as a fluid, the book writes the perfect-fluid components as a four-vector T^mu = (rho, p, p, p) rather than the diagonal rest-frame tensor T^{mu nu} = diag(rho, p, p, p).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Suggests the energy-momentum tensor has vector components and hides why comparing -Lambda g/8pi with it gives p = -rho (one needs g_00 = -1 flipping the sign of the 00 entry only).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write T^{mu nu} = diag(rho,p,p,p) in a local Minkowski frame, lower both indices with eta, and compare entry by entry with -Lambda eta_{mu nu}/8pi.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Margin note 10 states the comoving condition as the time derivative of r_ij(t0) vanishing, and margin note 14 contains a slip where S(t) = S'(t') is followed by S(t) = S(t') before concluding t = t'.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Notation is confusing: r(t0) is a constant by construction, and the scalar-clock argument reads as circular.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Define comoving labels x^i = r/a and say dx^i/dt = 0 for galaxies on the Hubble flow; restate the clock argument as: S is a scalar, so S'(t') = S(t') at the same event, and monotonic S forces t = t'.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'Every galaxy is running away from us. Does that mean we are at the centre?' Let the learner try, then build the stretching-lattice argument.
Second opener for stronger learners: 'Why should the weakest force decide the fate of the Universe?' Aim for range plus no cancellation.

Order: scale ladder and cosmological principle -> uniform scaling and H = a-dot/a -> comoving versus physical -> slices and fundamental observers -> metric form -> Universe 0 -> curvature of flat expanding metric -> Lambda source and exponential solution.
Check understanding: ask the learner to explain why the Solar System does not expand, and why the CMB dipole does not contradict relativity.
Check: 'If slices are flat, is spacetime flat?' Expect the answer no, backed by R = 6(ä/a + ȧ^2/a^2), which equals 12H^2 for de Sitter.
For index-shy learners, skip the orthonormal route and use the Christoffel symbols of eqn 15.33 to get R_00 and R_ii directly; for advanced learners, make them track each eta sign in 15.22.
When presenting negative pressure, avoid 'it pushes outward'; use the rho + 3p rule and flag that ch17 will derive it.
Common learner question: 'What is space expanding into?' Answer: nothing; a(t) describes changing distances within spacetime, and Fig. 15.5's outside is an artefact of drawing.
Common question: 'Is Hubble's constant really constant?' Answer: constant in space at fixed t, generally not in time; exactly constant only in de Sitter.
Common question: 'Where is the Big Bang in Universe 1?' a = e^{Ht} never vanishes; de Sitter has no initial singularity in these coordinates (though they do not cover all of de Sitter).
Use quick numbers to anchor scales: 1 pc ~ 3 ly, galaxy spacing ~ Mpc, homogeneity ~ 100 Mpc, Hubble time ~ 14 Gyr (derived from H0 = 70).
Correct the book's typos when writing equations aloud: -dt^2 in 15.32 and a(t0)^2 for the slice metric.
